reviews.one_line_contribution: A controlled dissociation, at matched rollout and token budgets, between transferring a reflective prompt optimizer's artifact (the optimized instruction skeleton) and transferring its accumulated diagnostic knowledge (a domain-scrubbed SYMPTOM/EDIT catalogue injected only into the reflection step), reported as a sample-efficiency Pareto curve with a crossover budget rather than a leaderboard win.
reviews.closest_prior_work: The Related Work engages GEPA, MIPROv2, PromptBreeder, REMO, SPoT/ATTEMPT and cross-model transfer, but omits the cluster that actually owns this idea: ExpeL (Zhao et al., AAAI 2024) already harvests cross-task insights from success/failure trajectories into a retrievable natural-language rule pool with explicit ADD/EDIT/DOWNVOTE operators and already evaluates transfer to unseen tasks; Dynamic Cheatsheet (2025) accumulates reusable strategies as persistent test-time memory; ReasoningBank (2025) distills generalizable strategies from both successful and failed traces into a retrieved memory; and Agentic Context Engineering (2025) literally builds an evolving 'playbook' of bullet-level strategies from execution feedback and benchmarks it against GEPA. Against these, 'harvest failure->edit rules, retrieve by symptom match, inject into context' is not the new thing. What survives as new is narrower: the injection point is the optimizer's reflection step rather than the executor's context, and the paper's real object is the artifact-vs-search-knowledge dissociation plus the crossover-budget measurement. That is a legitimate delta but it is a controlled-ablation delta, not a new mechanism, and the proposal does not currently frame it that way or cite the works it must beat.
reviews.strongest_objection: The design's own scrubbing gate maximizes the probability of its own null. Rules must pass a leakage test in which a held-out LLM cannot identify the source task above chance (<=1/6), and each rule is capped at 60 tokens. A 60-token instruction that is provably uninformative about which of six tasks produced it is, almost by construction, generic prompt-engineering advice — which is exactly baseline (iv), the hand-written checklist. Domain-generality and retained diagnostic specificity are in direct tension here, and the proposal treats scrubbing as a pass/fail hygiene step rather than as the dial that determines whether there is a paper. The likely interleaving that kills the central claim: playbook beats cold-start by 3-8 points at 50 rollouts, and the hand-written checklist matches it within the noise floor — at which point, by the authors' own refutation criterion, the harvesting contributes nothing and the result is 'putting any competent advice in the reflection prompt helps small-budget GEPA', which is not an ICLR contribution. Two supporting problems compound it. (a) Source/target contamination on the most favorable pair: 2WikiMultiHop is a source and HotpotQA is a target — near-duplicate multi-hop QA with near-identical failure modes and output format — and BBH subsets appear on both sides, so 'six held-out target tasks' overstates the transfer distance for at least three of them. (b) Half of the hypothesis ('never induce negative transfer', 'never worse than cold-start by more than the noise floor on any target') is an accept-the-null claim, but the statistical plan only powers a 1.5-point aggregate paired difference at n=30; per-target non-inferiority at n=5 seeds is badly underpowered and no equivalence test (TOST or comparable) is specified. Separately, the promised crossover CI 'narrower than the checkpoint spacing' is not identifiable from checkpoints at 25/50/100/200/300 when the crossover is predicted at 120-250 — the interval would be an artifact of interpolation between two checkpoints 100 rollouts apart.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: 1) Run baseline (iv), the hand-written checklist, as a two-target pilot BEFORE the full harvest, and make scrub strength a measured dial rather than a gate: report a leakage-vs-benefit curve (source-identification accuracy on the x-axis, gain over cold-start on the y-axis). If the curve is flat, that is the paper's finding and it is publishable; if it slopes, the harvested content is doing work and the claim is established. 2) Add the in-domain self-harvested playbook baseline (see missing_baseline). 3) Remove the contaminated pairs — move 2WikiMultiHop out of the source pool or HotpotQA out of the targets, and require that no target task shares a suite with any source task — then report gains as a function of stated source-target distance rather than pooled. 4) Specify a non-inferiority test with a pre-registered margin for the no-negative-transfer half of the hypothesis, and state per-target power honestly (or make that claim only at the pooled level). 5) Log test score continuously or at 8-10 checkpoints so the crossover budget is actually identifiable, and drop the promise that its CI beats the checkpoint spacing. 6) Cut the arm matrix to fit the stated budget (see feasibility) and say explicitly which arms run on all six targets and which run on a two-target subset. 7) Reposition against ExpeL / Dynamic Cheatsheet / ReasoningBank / ACE, and make the dissociation-and-crossover measurement the stated contribution rather than the playbook mechanism.
reviews.missing_baseline: An in-domain self-harvested playbook: run GEPA on the target task for the first 25-50 rollouts, distill a failure->edit playbook from that task's own traces by the identical pipeline, and inject it for the remaining budget — no cross-domain source runs at all. This is the baseline that decides whether 'cross-domain transfer' is the contribution or whether any failure->edit memory mechanism (REMO-style, same-domain) captures the entire effect, and it costs almost nothing relative to the rest of the matrix. Neither the shuffled-playbook control (isolates content vs token count) nor the hand-written checklist (isolates harvesting vs generic advice) covers it. A second, cheaper omission: cold-start GEPA given the same wall-clock/token budget spent on more reflection calls or longer reflections, since 'playbook helps' and 'more reflection compute helps' are confounded when the playbook lengthens the reflection prompt.
reviews.preprint_collision: The Preprint Collision Check field is empty — no searches are reported, so novelty is asserted rather than established, and I weight that as a weakness rather than a neutral. The Related Work does cite 2025-2026 items (REMO, PromptBridge, Oved et al.), so the authors are not ignoring recency wholesale, but they searched the prompt-optimizer literature and not the agent-memory literature, which is where the collision actually lives. Specific works the check should have surfaced and rebutted: Agentic Context Engineering (2025), which builds an incrementally updated 'playbook' of strategies from execution feedback and explicitly benchmarks against GEPA — the single most dangerous collision, since it shares the name, the object, and the comparison; ReasoningBank (2025), which distills reusable strategies from successful and failed trajectories into a retrieved memory; Dynamic Cheatsheet (2025), persistent test-time memory of reusable tactics; and ExpeL (2023/AAAI 2024), which already does cross-task insight extraction with transfer evaluation. None of these, to my knowledge, runs the artifact-vs-search-knowledge dissociation at matched budgets with a crossover interval, so the proposal is not dead — but the burden is now on the authors to run that comparison against a memory-augmented baseline from this cluster, not against stateless GEPA alone, and a submission that reaches reviewers without naming these will be scored as unaware of its own neighbourhood.

reviews.one_line_contribution: A controlled dissociation test showing that what transfers across domains in reflective prompt optimization is the optimizer's harvested failure-symptom-to-edit knowledge injected into GEPA's reflection step, not the optimized prompt skeleton, evaluated as a Pareto sample-efficiency curve with a measured crossover budget rather than a leaderboard win.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two clusters, only one of which the proposal engages. (a) REMO, which the proposal itself cites and correctly characterizes as a within-domain single-benchmark mistake notebook — the proposal's delta over it is cross-domain evaluation plus controls, i.e. an evaluation contribution, not a mechanism. (b) The cluster the proposal never mentions: ExpeL-style cross-task natural-language insight extraction from past success/failure pools (already claims transfer to unseen tasks), Dynamic Cheatsheet-style test-time strategy memory, and above all the 2025 agentic-context-engineering line that builds an incrementally curated 'playbook' of strategy bullets via a generator/reflector/curator loop and benchmarks it directly against GEPA. That last one uses the same word for the same object and already reports beating GEPA; the defensible difference here is that its playbook conditions the executor on domain-specific context whereas this one conditions the meta-level reflector on domain-scrubbed rules — a real but narrow distinction that the proposal has not articulated because it does not cite the work. A reviewer who knows that literature will read this as ExpeL/REMO lifted one level up the stack onto GEPA, which is exactly the 'domain swap' the track brief warns scores as a modest delta.
reviews.strongest_objection: The design cannot support the two claims it advertises as central, and this is visible from its own numbers. The Measurement section states per-run test SD ~3 points and n=30 paired observations detecting a 1.5-point mean paired difference at 80% power. The headline prediction then asserts (i) convergence to cold-start by 300 rollouts with a gap <=1.5 points, and (ii) 'playbook transfer is never worse than cold-start by more than the noise floor on any target'. Both are equivalence claims. (i) sits exactly at the MDE, so the study cannot distinguish 'converged' from 'still ahead by 1.4' or 'behind by 1.4' — the Pareto shape, which is the paper's whole framing, is asserted at the resolution limit of the instrument. (ii) is a per-target claim resting on 5 seeds each; with 6 targets and SD 3, at least one target showing a spurious 2-4 point deficit is the expected outcome, so the pre-registered refutation condition will most likely fire for reasons unrelated to the hypothesis and will have to be rescued post hoc. Compounding this, the prediction promises a crossover-budget bootstrap CI 'narrower than the checkpoint spacing' for a predicted crossover of 120-250 rollouts when the bracketing checkpoints are 100/200/300 — a crossover of two noisy monotone curves estimated from five discrete points with SD 3 will not yield an interval that tight, and claiming it in advance suggests the interval width was written as an aspiration rather than derived. This reproduces failure mode 2 from the track brief in a proposal that explicitly set out to avoid it.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Four changes. (1) Replace the equivalence assertions with a TOST-style pre-registered equivalence margin and power the 300-rollout convergence test and the per-target no-harm test for that margin — which will require more seeds per target (10-15) or fewer arms, and should be traded against the ablation list rather than added to it. (2) Pre-register the source-target distance partition before running: the current target set includes HotpotQA against a 2WikiMultiHop source and BBH-against-BBH-other-clusters, which are near-in-domain pairs that dilute the average and, worse, blunt the dissociation claim because the skeleton baseline should also succeed on them; report distant pairs as the primary analysis and near pairs separately. (3) Fix the compute arithmetic or cut the grid, and state the amortization argument explicitly: the playbook costs 6 sources x 300 rollouts x 3 seeds = 5,400 harvest rollouts, so give the break-even number of target tasks at which the transferred playbook is cheaper than cold-start, otherwise the sample-efficiency claim is only true after an unstated fixed cost. (4) Add a genuinely off-domain token-matched null (rules harvested for some unrelated skill) alongside the anti-matched shuffle, because with only 20-60 rules an anti-matched top-3 still returns on-topic prompt-optimization advice, so the shuffle control is likely to null out for the wrong reason and kill a live hypothesis.
reviews.missing_baseline: A within-run self-harvested playbook: run cold-start GEPA on the target task and accumulate the same SYMPTOM/EDIT rules from that run's own early failures and validated edit deltas, injected into its own later reflection calls, at matched rollouts and matched reflection tokens. This is the cheap competitor a practitioner would actually reach for, it requires no source harvesting at all, and if it matches cross-domain transfer then the entire harvesting apparatus and the transfer framing contribute nothing. The proposal's controls are all aimed at the wrong alternative: baseline (iv), the hand-written human checklist, tests whether the rules are generic, and the shuffled ablation tests whether content matters, but neither tests whether the knowledge needed to be imported from other domains rather than generated on the spot. A second cheap omission: a zero-rollout playbook generated by asking the same frontier reflection model to write 40 SYMPTOM/EDIT rules cold, formatted identically — a stronger and less sandbaggable version of the hand-written checklist. I would also expect a reviewer to demand plain best-of-N prompt sampling at matched rollouts, which is often competitive with reflective search at the 25-50 rollout budgets where this paper claims its win.
reviews.preprint_collision: The Preprint Collision Check field is empty. Judged on what the text actually provides, the Related Work section shows partial recency awareness — REMO is dated 2025 and a cross-tier transfer paper is dated 2026 — but it reports no searches, names no search scope or date window, and conspicuously omits the recent preprint line most likely to scoop it: 2025 agentic-context-engineering work that incrementally curates a reusable strategy 'playbook' through a reflector/curator loop and benchmarks it head-to-head against GEPA, plus ExpeL-style cross-task insight pools and Dynamic Cheatsheet-style test-time strategy memory. In a subfield where the threatening artifact is a three-month-old arXiv posting, an unsearched novelty claim over a neighborhood the track brief already flagged as crowded is a substantive weakness, not a neutral omission, and it is the main reason novelty is scored at 5 rather than 6-7 despite the genuinely good control set. The proposal must state which recent preprints it checked and articulate the meta-level (optimizer-conditioning) versus object-level (executor-conditioning) distinction explicitly, because that distinction is currently its only defensible novelty and it is not made anywhere in the text.

reviews.one_line_contribution: A controlled dissociation claiming that what transfers across domains in GEPA-style reflective prompt optimization is a harvested, domain-scrubbed SYMPTOM/EDIT rulebook injected into the reflection step — not the optimized prompt skeleton — reported as a matched-budget sample-efficiency Pareto curve with a measured crossover budget rather than a leaderboard win.
reviews.closest_prior_work: The proposal positions itself against GEPA/MIPROv2/PromptBreeder/REMO/SPoT, but the family that actually threatens it is cross-run experience reuse for LLM systems, which is not cited at all: ExpeL (Zhao et al., AAAI 2024) already extracts natural-language insights from training-task trajectories into a retrieved insight pool and reports transfer to unseen tasks; AutoGuide (NeurIPS 2024) already induces state-conditioned 'situation -> guideline' rules from offline experience and retrieves them by match — structurally identical to SYMPTOM/EDIT retrieval by embedding similarity; Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2025) is a test-time memory of reusable strategies carried across tasks; and ACE / agentic context-engineering work (2025) literally builds and incrementally curates an evolving 'playbook' of bullets from execution feedback with a reflector/curator split. Against these, 'harvest failure->edit rules, scrub, retrieve, inject into the reflector' is not a new mechanism. REMO, which the proposal does cite, is dismissed for being single-benchmark and making no transfer claim — that is an evaluation delta, and the brief explicitly warns that a domain/eval swap scored as a modest delta rather than a contribution. What is genuinely new here is narrower than the title: the head-to-head artifact-vs-search-knowledge dissociation under a shared noise floor and matched token budget. That is a well-designed measurement of someone else's mechanism, not a new one.
reviews.strongest_objection: The central dissociation is guaranteed by the analysis plan rather than tested by it. The Falsifiable Predictions section asserts (a) prompt-skeleton warm start 'loses 2-5 points on distant pairs' and (b) playbook transfer 'is never worse than cold-start by more than the noise floor on any target'. Claim (b) is a null, and the Measurement section pre-declares an MDE of 1.5 points at n=30 plus a rule that 'effects below the null-replicate floor will be reported as null regardless of p-value'. So the playbook arm cannot be found to hurt unless it hurts by more than the design's own detection threshold, while the skeleton arm is predicted to hurt by an amount comfortably above it. Two separate one-sided conclusions at asymmetric power are not a dissociation; the paper needs the arm x source-target-distance interaction, powered for the interaction, and an equivalence test with a stated margin for 'never worse'. Three further defects compound this. (i) Experiment 6, the negative-transfer probe, transfers from a single distant source (symbolic BBH only) for both arms, but the headline playbook arm is built from six sources — so the probe's playbook has far fewer rules and different composition than the arm whose safety is being claimed, and 'which source' is confounded with 'how many rules'; the ablation 'playbook from one source domain vs six' concedes this axis matters. (ii) The shuffled-playbook control retrieves rules by anti-matching symptoms at identical token count. Anti-matched advice is plausibly worse than no advice (it misdirects the reflector), so this control can sit below cold-start and inflate the content-vs-conditioning contrast; the correct control is randomly-matched rules from the same pool. (iii) The crossover-budget promise — 'a bootstrap CI narrower than the checkpoint spacing' — is not supportable from the stated variance. Checkpoints are 25/50/100/200/300 and the crossover is predicted at 120-250, i.e. inside a single 100-rollout gap where the identification is pure interpolation, and a crossover is the ratio of a shrinking difference to a shrinking slope, whose bootstrap distribution with per-run SD ~3 and 30 paired observations will be wide or unbounded. Finally, the scrubbing loop is in tension with the paper's own value proposition: rules that fail the 6-way source-identification test are 're-scrubbed or dropped', which systematically selects the playbook toward generic, domain-free advice — precisely the direction that makes baseline (iv), the hand-written checklist, match it, which the proposal itself designates as the refutation condition.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: 1) Restate the headline as a pre-registered interaction: fit arm (playbook / skeleton) x distance (near / far) with task random effects, power the interaction rather than the two simple effects, and replace 'never worse than cold-start' with a TOST equivalence test against a stated margin. 2) Match the negative-transfer probe to the headline condition — run both a six-source and a one-source playbook against the six-source and one-source skeletons, so composition is not confounded with source distance. 3) Swap the anti-matched shuffle for randomly-matched rules from the same pool, and add an LLM-authored, unharvested rulebook matched in count, length, and format (see missing baseline). 4) Fix the budget arithmetic: cut arms (drop the SPoT-style soft-prompt reference and MIPROv2, which the brief already scopes out as a baseline-not-method) and spend the savings on seeds and on intermediate checkpoints at 75/150 so the crossover is bracketed rather than interpolated; report the crossover only when adjacent-checkpoint CIs actually separate, and otherwise report AUBC alone. 5) Report the leakage-test attrition rate and the pre/post-scrub playbooks as separate arms — if aggressive scrubbing is what makes rules safe, the harvesting claim is weaker than the framing. 6) Add an explicit preprint search over the experience-reuse/agent-memory family and state, rule by rule, what the harvested playbook contains that ExpeL-style insight pools and playbook-curation methods do not.
reviews.missing_baseline: An unharvested but format-matched rulebook: ask the same frontier reflection model to write 20-60 domain-general SYMPTOM/EDIT rules of <=60 tokens each, with no source runs, no traces, and no validated deltas, then retrieve and inject them by the identical top-3 embedding procedure. Baseline (iv) — a hand-written 'good prompting practices' checklist — is not this: it is human-authored, unmatched in count, length, and retrieval mechanism, and injected statically, so a win over it confounds 'harvesting from real runs' with 'having a retrieved, structured rulebook at all'. Since the entire cost and the entire claim of the paper is the harvesting (steps 2-3), the arm that isolates it is mandatory, not optional. Secondary omissions a reviewer will also raise: (a) a demonstration-only small-budget arm (bootstrapped few-shot selection, stopped at 25-50 rollouts), which is the strongest practical competitor exactly in the regime where the Pareto claim lives and which MIPROv2-at-full-budget does not stand in for; (b) an ExpeL / Dynamic-Cheatsheet-style memory baseline, i.e. the competing method family rather than a straw control; (c) a zero-rollout arm (playbook applied once to the seed prompt, no search), which bounds how much of the 50-rollout gain is search at all.
reviews.preprint_collision: The Preprint Collision Check field is empty, and nothing elsewhere in the submission substitutes for it: the Related Work section names indexed or well-known systems (GEPA, MIPROv2, PromptBreeder, SPoT/ATTEMPT, APE) plus two citations given without venue and unverifiable as written ('REMO, Wu & Qu, 2025' and 'PromptBridge / Oved et al., 2026'), and reports no searches, no date window, and no search terms. That is an unsearched claim of novelty and I score it as a weakness, not a neutral — especially given that the proposal's own citation list already reaches into 2026, i.e. exactly the fast-moving preprint layer it did not systematically check. Concretely, the search that was not run would have surfaced the collision: ExpeL (cross-task natural-language insight extraction and retrieval, with transfer experiments), AutoGuide (automatically induced context-conditioned guidelines selected by situation match), Dynamic Cheatsheet (persistent cross-task strategy memory at test time), Agent Workflow Memory (induced reusable routines carried to new tasks), and the 2025 agentic-context-engineering line that builds and curates an evolving 'playbook' of feedback-derived bullets with a reflector/curator split — the last of which uses the proposal's own central noun for the same object. I cannot certify that any single one of these already states this exact Pareto/dissociation claim on GEPA at matched rollout budgets, and I do not believe one does; the mechanism, however, is clearly not new, and the burden of showing otherwise was the proposal's and was not discharged. Until the authors run and report that search, the novelty score has to be set by the mechanism rather than by the framing.
